section: Define Success Before Looking for a Winner
text:
Define Success Before Looking for a Winner
Primary outcome: mean two-week sales per assigned customer, in dollars.
Secondary outcomes: purchase conversion and website visit rates.
For campaign \(a\) and no-email control \(0\):
\[\widehat{\Delta}_a = \overline{Y}_a - \overline{Y}_0\]
\(Y_i\) is customer \(i\)’s two-week spending, including zero purchases. Positive \(\widehat{\Delta}_a\) estimates additional sales per assigned customer.
Check: the denominator includes every customer assigned to that arm.

Analyze assignment as an intention-to-treat comparison. Independent arm means, not paired customer differences. Random assignment supports a causal comparison for this experiment, assuming valid implementation and no interference. There is no basis for conditioning on email opens, visitors, or purchasers.

One Source, Three Report Formats
In report.qmd, the coding agent selects PDF (via Typst) and Word:
format:
  typst: default        # writes report.pdf
  docx: default
bibliography: context/sources.bib
jupyter: python3
Typst is bundled with Quarto: no LaTeX install, the same engine as the workshop’s PDFs. The notebook conversion preserves Markdown and executable Python cells. Ask the agent to include readable reference links in the notebook.

Quarto includes the Typst CLI, so no separate installation is needed, and typst output is a PDF named after the source: report.pdf (https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html, checked 2026-10-30). Typst processes the citations itself and prints its own “Bibliography” heading, so the report should not add a second “References” heading; set citeproc: true only if a CSL style is required. Tested on 2026-10-30 with Quarto 1.6.40 in a disposable copy of the lab inputs: the PDF listed both references, the DOCX rendered the citations, and the notebook route executed.

    n=("spend", "size"), sales=("spend", "mean"),

title: AI Workflows for Quarto
text:
What Does Uncertainty Mean Here?
⭐ self-paced

Explain the assumptions behind the intervals. For independent arms, use customer-level sampling and preserve assignment groups. Compare men's and women's emails directly before declaring a winner. State how multiple comparisons and skewed spending affect interpretation.

Check: most customers spend zero; a few spend much more. Intervals describe estimation uncertainty under stated assumptions.

Do not use paired resampling: each customer receives one assignment. A bootstrap can sample customer rows separately within each arm and recompute each contrast; state the seed, repetitions, independence assumption, and interval method. A normal approximation needs a justification for highly skewed spending. If using many subgroup comparisons, label them exploratory and plan validation. Neither an interval nor randomization establishes applicability to a new retailer.

📚 All Quarto output formats · Quarto logo: Posit, PBC

text:
🧠 Model + 🔧 Harness = 🤖 Assistant


🧠
Model
reads and writes text, asks for tools


🔧
Harness
files, commands, permissions


🤖
Coding assistant
model + harness in your terminal



📏 Bigger, newer model → usually better on hard tasks
🪶 Small models: fast, cheap, may stumble on multi-step work
✅ Enough today: Haiku or Sonnet on medium · Sol on low

💬 Which would you pick to fix a typo, and which to join two datasets?


The model is the language model (for example Claude, GPT or Gemini). The harness is the program around it: it gives the model tools to read and write files, run commands and search, asks you to approve actions, and feeds results back in a loop. Assistants such as the three on the next slide are harnesses; many can run several models, so the same harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently in a different harness. Size and quality matter per task: larger, more recent models usually follow longer instructions, plan multi-step work, and recover from errors better, while small models are quicker and cheaper and are often enough for short, well-specified edits such as fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Hard tasks here, such as joining datasets or debugging a failed render, reward the stronger model. Quality is not only size: training and recency matter too, and no model is always right, so check its work (the “you direct and check” rule). Good answer to the check: a small model for the typo, the strongest available for the join. If a prompt keeps failing, try a stronger model inside your assistant (see its documentation for how). Model names and availability change often; do not name versions on stage. For this workshop the prompts are short and well specified, so Haiku or Sonnet with the effort (reasoning) setting on medium, or ChatGPT’s Sol on low, is sufficient; try a stronger model or higher effort only if a prompt keeps failing.

text:
📜 Using AI in Research: Say It, Own It
🏠 before the workshop


🚫
Never an author
AI cannot be accountable


🔍
You verify everything
code, numbers, references


🔒
Keep private data out
unpublished or sensitive work stays out of public tools


📝
Disclose the use
tool + version · task · your checks



⚖️ Never generate or alter primary data or images: that is misconduct

Publishers’ policies differ, so read the one for your journal, course or employer before submitting. The common core, from the summary supplied for this deck (not yet checked against each publisher’s own policy page: do that before teaching, and record the date): AI tools are not listed as authors because they cannot take responsibility; the authors verify AI output, including facts and references, and answer for plagiarism; unpublished manuscripts, review reports, participant data and proprietary work are not uploaded to public AI tools. Where to disclose depends on the use. Basic copyediting (grammar, spelling) is usually exempt. Drafting or translating text goes in the acknowledgements or a declaration, with the tool and version. Data analysis and coding go in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce them. Explanatory diagrams are disclosed in the caption or declaration. Generating or altering primary research images or raw data is prohibited. Publishers also differ in form: some ask for a separate AI declaration with the submission, some for a note in the cover letter, and some ban AI-generated images outright. This workshop is a reason to practise: you direct an assistant, so you will have something to disclose. The next slide shows a statement.

Good answer to the check: a typo fix is basic copyediting and is usually exempt; computing a table is analysis and belongs in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce it, which here is the code and the AGENTS.md that the project keeps.

🧰 Environments: Then and Now


💻
OS
macOS · Windows · Linux


🔩
Chip
Intel/AMD x86_64 · Apple/ARM arm64

Language
Python · R · JS … which version?

Dependencies
packages · versions · compiled C

conda · compilers · PATH · kernels → ⏳ hours


⚡
Now 🐍 uv
🔒 one lockfile, every OS and chip → ⏱️ seconds



🤖 either way: the assistant sets it up · you approve


Code runs on an operating system and a chip, in some version of its language, with packages at particular versions. That holds for most languages, not just Python. Many scientific packages contain compiled C, C++ or Fortran, built separately for each OS and chip: Python ships them as wheels whose platform tag names both, such as macosx_11_0_arm64 (“compatibility with macOS 11 or later”) or manylinux_…_x86_64 (https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/platform-compatibility-tags/). Setting this up used to be a lesson of its own: install conda or a system Python, sometimes a compiler, fix PATH, register a Jupyter kernel, then debug it on each laptop. For Python, uv now does it in one step. It fetches Python too (“uv automatically installs missing Python versions as needed”, https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/install-python/), and uv.lock “captures the packages that would be installed across all possible Python markers such as operating system, architecture, and Python version” (https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/layout/), so one lockfile serves every Mac, Windows and Linux laptop in the room. Other languages pair a project file with a lockfile the same way: R’s renv.lock (https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html), npm’s package-lock.json (https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-lock-json) and Rust’s Cargo.lock (https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html); all checked 2026-10-31. Either way, nobody needs to remember the commands: say what the project needs, and the assistant runs them while you approve. The next slide does exactly that. Claude Code · Codex · Antigravity · checked 2026-10-31

A sub-agent is a separate assistant session that the lead starts for one task: it has its own context window, does the task and reports back, while the lead waits for all of them and checks the results. Independent tasks then take about as long as the slowest one, but each sub-agent does its own model and tool work, so a run uses more tokens. Claude Code runs sub-agents in parallel when a prompt asks for them, without any set-up; its own example is “Research the authentication, database, and API modules in parallel using separate subagents” (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). Codex enables sub-agents by default and starts them when asked; its docs warn that parallel edits “can create conflicts” and that sub-agent runs use more tokens (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents). Antigravity’s CLI lets its primary agent delegate to parallel subagents (https://antigravity.google/docs/subagents?tab=cli); the docs do not say a prompt can require it, so agy may do the tasks itself. All checked 2026-10-31. Two rules keep parallel work safe, and the prompt states both: each sub-agent writes only its own files and renders nothing, and the lead renders the files one at a time, because two Quarto renders, or two uv run environment updates, in one folder can collide. Sub-agents read AGENTS.md too, so the project’s rules (cited numbers, open photos, uv run) still apply. This is the same split as this repository’s own role contracts in its AGENTS.md.

🌳 Git: Every Change, Safely

🕰️ every saved version kept · 🐙 shared on GitHub



🌿
branch
main stays untouched


💾
commit
a snapshot + why


☁️
push
copy it to GitHub


🔀

propose the change


👀
review

✅

into main



👤 today: straight to main · 👥 a team: the whole loop


Concepts, not commands: the assistant runs git and you approve. The six terms stay in English when the deck is translated, as they do in git and on GitHub. A repository is the project folder plus its full history. A commit is a snapshot of every tracked file with a message saying why, so any earlier version can be restored or compared. A branch is a movable label on a line of commits: work happens on a branch while main stays working (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Branches-in-a-Nutshell). Push copies commits to the remote repository on GitHub. A pull request proposes merging a branch, shows the diff and collects discussion and checks (https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests); a review comments on it, approves it or asks for changes (https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/reviewing-changes-in-pull-requests/about-pull-request-reviews); merging adds its commits to main. All checked 2026-10-31. Working alone today, the next slides commit straight to main and push; in a team, every change goes round the loop, and this workshop’s own repository is built that way. Ask the assistant to “commit with a message that says why”, and read its diffs before you approve.

A white paper is the academic version of the guide: abstract, introduction, methods, results, conclusions and references, with every number computed from data/ (the project’s AGENTS.md says so, so the prompt need not). It looks like a LaTeX article without a LaTeX install: Quarto 1.10.20 bundles Typst 0.15, which embeds New Computer Modern, the OpenType version of LaTeX’s Computer Modern (checked 2026-11-01 in the PDF’s embedded fonts). The paper’s header needs Quarto ≥ 1.10 (quarto --version): 1.6.40 stops with “unexpected argument: spacing”. section-numbering numbers the headings, bibliography reads the BibTeX file, and bibliographystyle: ieee picks Typst’s numbered style. Typst prints its own “Bibliography” heading, so the prompt asks for #set bibliography(title: [References]), which goes in the Typst format’s include-in-header; the paper then needs no References heading of its own. The finished example also wraps Quarto’s Typst article function so that the title is set in New Computer Modern too. [@key] cites a reference; @fig-…, @tbl-…, @eq-… and @sec-… refer to labelled figures, tables, equations and sections. An inline expression in a YAML abstract runs before the setup cell and fails, so the finished example writes its abstract in the body, wrapped in a raw {=typst} block. It also floats figures, draws booktabs-style table rules and sizes table columns to their contents (tbl-colwidths: false). ALVA counts only its members, so the paper says “ALVA member attractions” and treats the five sights as a description, not a sample. Genuine LaTeX output is format: pdf, which needs a TeX distribution (quarto install tinytex): https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/pdf-basics.html. All sources are public Colombian open data, joined on the DANE DIVIPOLA municipality code (see examples/water/data/README.md for every table, licence and cut-off date). INS (Instituto Nacional de Salud) publishes the IRCA surveillance results (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3); DANE supplies the list of municipalities, population projections and boundaries (and the population behind per-person spending); the IRCA table is the utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA, not INS’s national total; ICFES supplies the Saber 11 exam and MEN the school dropout rate. DNP, CHIRPS and SRTM add poverty, spending, rainfall and altitude. Why it is useful: drinking-water quality is a public-health issue, but national averages hide where the risk is. Municipal data lets us see which places and which zones (urban or rural) are worst, and compare them with outcomes such as infant mortality and exam scores. Because the data and the analysis are open, anyone can check and rebuild the results, which is the point of this workshop.

title: Quarto Workshop
text:
📏 Two Measures: IRCA and Saber 11


💧 IRCA · water-safety risk

🧪 tap-water samples against health limits
⚖️ failed tests weighted by risk: E. coli 25 · turbidity 15 · pH 1.5
📏 0 = no risk → 100 = unfit



🎓 Saber 11 · ICFES exam

🧑‍🎓 students finishing secondary school
📚 5 tests: reading, maths, social studies, science, English
📏 global score 0–500




🧮 both are averages: IRCA over water samples · Saber 11 over students

Resolución 2115 de 2007, arts. 13–14 (normas.cra.gov.co) · ICFES, Saber 11.° Guía de orientación 2017-1, pp. 101 and 104 (icfes.gov.co)

IRCA (Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano), Resolución 2115 de 2007: each tested characteristic carries a risk score (art. 13, Cuadro 6: Escherichia coli 25, total coliforms 15, turbidity 15, free residual chlorine 15, apparent colour 6, pH 1.5, among others). A sample’s IRCA is the score of the characteristics that fail their limit as a percentage of the score of all characteristics analysed, and the monthly IRCA is the mean over the month’s samples (art. 14). So 0 means every test passed and 100 means every test failed. Our irca is the year’s utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA from the INS open table; the next slide shows why that matters. Saber 11 is ICFES’s standardized exam for students finishing upper secondary school, with five tests (critical reading, mathematics, social studies and citizenship, natural sciences, English). The global score is 5 × the weighted mean of the five test scores (each 0–100; English weight 1, the others 3), on 0–500 without decimals, and its mean was fixed at 250 in the first sitting (2014-2) so that years compare (guide, p. 104). Our saber11_mean is the mean global score of the students whose school is in that municipality and zone, both sittings of a year pooled; it covers only students who sat the exam, so it says nothing about those who left school. Sources checked 2026-10-30.

🧩 k-Means in Four Steps

● point◉ centre⏸ fix12345678🎲 1🎲 2🎲 3🧩 This 3-D view needs WebGL; the four steps are written in the notes.

① drop 3 centres at random points



🎯 goal: points close to their centre · 🧭 why? many rows → a few kinds you can read, compare and act on

🎬 Short · ¿Qué es k-means?


💧 water data: k = 4 is a hyperparameter, picked from k = 2–8 by an elbow rule · silhouette stays low (about 0.2), so k is a judgement call


Synthetic toy points, labelled as such: 120 random points in 3-D around three centres, drawn by this deck with a fixed seed. The four steps: ① drop k centres at random points; ② assign every point to its nearest centre; ③ move each centre to the mean of its points; ④ repeat ② and ③ until nothing changes. → steps through the algorithm; the numbered buttons jump to a step, ▶ play runs it, 🎲 1–3 pick one of three random starts (two reach the lowest inertia, the third gets stuck: a bad start can give a worse answer, hence n_init=20), and dragging turns the cloud. The lines are the distances that inertia adds up.
Why cluster? (1) A table of thousands of rows becomes a few kinds a person can read and name. (2) You can compare and target by kind: which places need which help. (3) It needs no labels, so it is a first look at data nobody has categorised. (4) Odd groups point to data errors or special cases. Clusters describe; they do not explain or prove causes.
🎬 The Short “But What is K-Means?” (Graduate ML, https://youtube.com/shorts/H1kB2FAjePw) opens in a player that sets 0.9× speed (checked: the player reports 0.9) and requests Spanish captions and interface. YouTube’s embed has no setting, documented or otherwise, for the audio language, so choose Spanish audio in the player’s ⚙ menu (Audio track) if the video offers it; an unavailable track is not an error here (checked 2026-11-03: none was exposed).
k-means needs k up front. It starts from k centres, assigns each point to the nearest, moves each centre to the mean of its points, and repeats until nothing changes. Different starts can end in different solutions, so we run 20 starts (n_init=20) and keep the best, with a fixed random_state for reproducibility. Inertia is the sum of squared distances from points to their centre.
Choosing k for the water data (choose_k() in analysis.py, fitted on all kept rows): k = 2 is excluded because it mostly splits urban from rural rows (adjusted Rand index with the zone 0.50). Elbow: take the smallest k ≥ 3 after which one more cluster cuts inertia by less than 10%, if its silhouette is within 0.01 of the best k ≥ 3. Here the next cluster cuts inertia by only 7% and the silhouette (−1 to 1, on a fixed sample of 5,000 rows) is 0.195. A silhouette near 0.2 is weak: the kinds overlap and summarise a continuum, which is normal for social data. Stability: refits with 5 other seeds give the same clusters (adjusted Rand index ≥ 0.998; 1 means perfect agreement). The elbow and silhouette plots are on clusters.qmd.

Confounders affect both water safety and health: poorer and more rural places have worse water and worse access to clinics, and they also register fewer births and deaths. text:
✍️🌐 3:00 · Blog + Website


# _quarto.yml
project:
  type: website
  execute-dir: project
  pre-render: scripts/analysis.py
execute:
  freeze: false

# index.qmd
listing:
  contents: posts
🔁 pre-render rebuilds outputs/
🧪 freeze: false re-runs every page → always the new numbers


⭐ later, for slow sites: freeze: auto reuses old results
until you run rm -rf _freeze


pre-render runs the script before every render, including a single-file render inside the project. freeze: false re-executes every page on every render, so one uv run quarto render rebuilds the analysis and every publication, and nothing needs clearing when data/ or the script change. execute-dir: project makes every page, including the post in posts/…/, read outputs/ and data/ from the project folder. Optional extension for slow sites: freeze: auto stores each page’s results in _freeze/ and re-executes a page only when its own source changes, so changes to data/ or outputs/ are not detected; delete _freeze/ (or render that page directly, which ignores freeze) after the data or the analysis change. A listing turns posts/*/index.qmd into a blog index. Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/projects/scripts.html, https://quarto.org/docs/projects/code-execution.html#freeze, https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-listings.html (checked 2026-10-30).

The workshop’s second task without a supplied prompt, and the one that checks the lesson of the block: the analysis runs once and every publication reads its outputs/. The setting MAX_MISSING drops rows missing more than that many features. $$
W = \sum_c \sum_i \|z_i - m_c\|^2
$$ {#eq-kmeans}

k-means [@lloyd1982] minimises @eq-kmeans.

Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/examples/water/README.md

The same article format as Part 1’s white paper (#london-whitepaper): Typst styled like a LaTeX article, with no LaTeX install; #set bibliography(title: [References]) goes in the Typst format’s include-in-header, so the paper needs no References heading of its own. An inline expression in a YAML abstract fails (it runs before the setup cell), hence “no inline code”. New here are equations: $$ … $$ {#eq-kmeans} numbers an equation and @eq-kmeans refers to it. The methods cite the papers behind each step: k-means, Lloyd (1982), https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1982.1056489; the silhouette, Rousseeuw (1987), https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-0427(87)90125-7; the adjusted Rand index, Hubert and Arabie (1985), https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01908075; and scikit-learn, Pedregosa et al. (2011), https://jmlr.org/papers/v12/pedregosa11a.html (all checked 2026-11-01). An assistant can invent a plausible reference, so the prompt asks it to check every DOI; ask it to drop any it cannot open rather than guess. The project’s AGENTS.md supplies the rules the prompt leaves out: the utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA label, every number from outputs/, outcomes never clustered on, and comparisons that are descriptive, not causal. The finished paper, quarto-workshop/examples/water/whitepaper.qmd, also cites the WHO drinking-water fact sheet and Robinson (1950) on ecological correlation. Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html and https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html (checked 2026-11-01).
